documents.title: What one flipped bit costs on the ET-SoC-1
documents.group: Flips to watts: the E60-E64 series
documents.summary: One flipped input bit of an fp32 multiply-add costs 117 fJ of board energy, a read-port bit 20.8 fJ, a result bit 31.2 fJ. The same 4,096 multiply-adds cost 0.68 W more in max-flip order than in Gray order, and the price follows voltage squared.

documents.title: A bit flip in microns: the 10 micrometre rule, measured
documents.group: Flips to watts: the E60-E64 series
documents.summary: Bill Dally's rule read per flipped bit is 10 micrometres. Here a flipped bit is worth about 5 as a gate's toggle, 0.3 mm as an operand bit delivered to a gate, and 1.8 mm as a multiply-add input bit.

documents.title: Verifying the deterministic transistor-flip experiments
documents.group: Flips to watts: the E60-E64 series
documents.summary: Seven proposed experiments pre-registered and run on three cards. A result bit costs 27 to 30 fJ, not 44; a carry position about 1 fJ, not 14; the vector multiply-add has no zero gate. Of 15 registered rows, 1 confirmed and 4 refuted.

documents.title: Power, then heat: what limits the ET-SoC-1's matmul speed
documents.group: Flips to watts: the E60-E64 series
documents.summary: Both of the governor’s limits act, each on its own. On a cool die the 65 W power test alone sets the clock, so zeros run 13% faster than random fp32 data. At a 66 C reading the thermal test alone. In sustained work heat wins and zeros run 33% faster.
